summary: Describes the flow and service information model for Deterministic Networking, defined for IP and MPLS DetNet data planes. It provides a common way to describe flows and the services they need.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist form describing a time-critical data stream and the guarantees it needs, so every tool fills it in the same way.

questions: what information describes a detnet flow
subtitle: A common vocabulary for describing deterministic network flows and the guarantees they require.

tldr.problem: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) provides services with guaranteed low loss and bounded latency, but operators and implementors need a standard way to describe flows and their requirements.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9016 defines information models for DetNet flows and services, specifying how to describe flow characteristics (identification, traffic specification, endpoints, rank), requirements (bandwidth, latency, loss), and service delivery profiles using consistent terminology.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides a common framework aligned with IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) to enable DetNet across both IP and MPLS networks, supporting interoperability between implementations.

facts.label: IP 6-tuple components
facts.value: Source IP, destination IP, DSCP, protocol, source port, destination port

today: RFC 9016 is an Informational RFC published in March 2021 that provides the information model framework for DetNet. The RFC remains the current standard for describing DetNet flows and services. RFC 8655 (Architecture), RFC 8938 (Data Plane Framework), RFC 8939 (IP Data Plane), and RFC 8964 (MPLS Data Plane) are the normative references for the underlying DetNet specifications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) provides the capability to carry specified data flows for real-time applications with extremely low packet loss and assured maximum end-to-end delivery latency. DetNet can operate over IP or MPLS networks, and is aligned with IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) for Layer 2 networks.

RFC 9016 describes the flow and service information models that users, operators, and implementors use to understand and configure DetNet services. These are not data models or configuration specifications; they are conceptual frameworks for how information should be structured. A DetNet flow may contain one or more application-level flows (App-flows), and multiple DetNet flows may share a single DetNet service.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet is a way to guarantee that time-critical data gets through the network on time. This document explains what information you need to describe a flow and what it needs.

sections.title: Information Elements
sections.content:
The information models rely on three groups of parameters. App-flow-related parameters describe the characteristics and requirements of the original application traffic: identification, encapsulation format (Ethernet, MPLS, or IP), data flow specification, traffic specification, endpoints, status, and rank. An App-flow can be an Ethernet frame, an MPLS packet, or an IP packet.

DetNet flow-related parameters describe the DetNet flow itself after DetNet encapsulation has been applied. These include management ID, payload type, format (MPLS or IP), flow specification, traffic specification, endpoints, rank, status, and requirements.

DetNet service-related parameters describe the service offered by the network for one or more DetNet flows: service ID, delivery type, delivery profile (bandwidth, latency, loss guarantees), connectivity type (point-to-point or point-to-multipoint), bidirectional requirements, rank, and status.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has three parts: what the application data looks like, what the network will do to it, and what guarantees the network makes.

sections.title: Flow Identification and Traffic Specification
sections.content:
DetNet flows can be identified using different mechanisms depending on the underlying technology. For MPLS flows, identification uses the MPLS switching label (SLabel) and the label stack. For IP flows, identification uses a 6-tuple of source IP address, destination IP address, DSCP value, protocol number, source port, and destination port. Additional optional identifiers include the IPv6 flow label and IPSec SPI.

The traffic specification describes how the ingress transmits packets: the transmission interval (in nanoseconds), maximum and minimum packets per interval, and maximum and minimum payload sizes. These parameters allow resource allocation to handle both constant bitrate (CBR) and variable bitrate (VBR) flows. Traffic exceeding the specification may receive degraded service; policing and shaping mechanisms can mitigate excess traffic from malicious or malfunctioning devices.
sections.plainLanguage: You describe a flow by labeling it (in MPLS) or by its address, port, and protocol (in IP). Then you say how much traffic to expect per second and how big the packets are.

sections.title: Service Requirements and Delivery Profile
sections.content:
DetNet defines six key performance parameters for both flows and services. Minimum Bandwidth (in octets per second) ensures sufficient capacity. Maximum Latency (in nanoseconds) sets an upper bound on end-to-end delivery time. Maximum Latency Variation (jitter, in nanoseconds) limits the difference between the fastest and slowest packets.

Maximum Loss specifies the acceptable packet loss rate. Maximum Consecutive Loss is important for applications that cannot tolerate losing consecutive packets (e.g., losing frames 1, 2, and 3 in sequence is worse than losing frames 1, 3, and 5). Maximum Misordering constrains out-of-order delivery; a value of zero requires strict in-order delivery.

The flow rank (0-255, where 0 is highest priority) determines which flows are removed if network resources become exhausted. Bidirectional requirements allow flows to request that forward and reverse paths use the same nodes and links for synchronous operation.
sections.plainLanguage: You list what you need: enough speed, time limits, acceptable losses, and whether packets must arrive in order. You give important flows a higher priority number so they don't get dropped first if the network gets congested.

sections.title: Flow and Service Status
sections.content:
The information model tracks the status of flows and services through their lifecycle. DnFlowStatus includes separate ingress and egress status indicators. The ingress can be None, Ready, Failed, or OutOfService. The egress can report Ready (all egresses operational), PartialFailed (some egresses working), Failed (all egresses down), or OutOfService.

Failure codes describe the reason for failure, such as packet replication and elimination being requested but not supported, or an ingress or egress failure. DetNet service status similarly reports whether the service instance is ready for use. Join, Leave, and Modify operations allow flows to enter, exit, or reconfigure services dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: The system keeps track of whether each flow is working, partially working, or broken, and why. Flows can be added, removed, or adjusted while running.
